front: What is a bystander in Holocaust history?
back: A person or government that knew, or could have known, what was happening and neither took part nor tried to stop it.
Hebrew for 'standing up': Yehuda Bauer's term for a broad definition of Jewish resistance, including hiding and keeping records as well as armed revolt.

front: What did Browning argue in Ordinary Men (1992)?
back: That ordinary middle-aged policemen of Reserve Police Battalion 101 killed Jews because of conformity, obedience and careerism as well as propaganda.
That a widespread eliminationist antisemitism in German society drove ordinary Germans to kill; most historians rejected the claim as too general.

front: What was the roundup of 16-17 July 1942 in Paris?
back: French police arrested thousands of Jews under arrangements with the Germans.

front: What was the War Refugee Board?
back: An American agency set up in January 1944 to help rescue victims of Nazi persecution; it helped to save tens of thousands.

front: Why is the definition of Jewish resistance debated?
back: Some limit it to armed revolt; others include hiding, escape and keeping records; critics fear that a broad definition loses meaning.

front: Should other victims be included in the term Holocaust?
back: Some limit it to the Jews because of the aim to murder every Jew; others include Roma, disabled people and others; many take a middle position.

front: Why did the Allies not do more to rescue Jews?
back: Priority to winning the war, restrictive immigration policies, disbelief and prejudice; historians disagree about what was possible.
